title: Session: 'stress and insomnia' after his business closed

client.name: Tom Becker
client.presentation: {distress >= 6 ? "Slumped, staring at his hands" : distress >= 3 ? "Tired, speaking slowly" : "A little lighter, sitting up"}; {rapport >= 6 ? "he is talking with you" : rapport >= 3 ? "he is guarded" : "he has shut down"}.

brief.situation: You are a licensed professional counselor at a community counseling center. Tom Becker, 52 (a fictional client), is here for a first session; his intake form says 'stress and insomnia'. He owned a print shop for 20 years until it closed four months ago. You have 50 minutes.
handover: Intake form: married, two children in college; 'can't sleep, can't shut my brain off'; no past counseling; no medicines listed.
The center's consent form, signed today, explains the limits of confidentiality, including risk of harm.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Tom answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His rapport, distress and how much he discloses change with what you say. What he tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 50 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation and document.

source.cite: Common outpatient practice: a 50-minute session (the 'therapy hour')
source.note: Author's scenario timing; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

checkIn.label: Open-ended check-in: 'What brings you in, in your own words?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give the client room to answer.

effects.finding: "My wife made me come. I can't sleep. Stress, I guess. The shop closed in July."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Tom nods slowly. "Twenty years. Then just gone."

askChanges.label: Ask what else has changed since the shop closed: sleep, appetite, energy, interest in things he used to enjoy

effects.log: You ask about the rest of his days since July.

effects.finding: "I wake at three and that's it. Not hungry. Tired all day. I haven't been fishing since spring, and that was my thing."

askNights.label: Ask what goes through his mind when he lies awake

effects.log: You ask what his mind does at three in the morning.

effects.finding: "Every decision. If I'd taken the loan. If I'd gone digital sooner. Round and round, for hours. It doesn't solve anything."

effects.log: Ruminative thinking: repetitive, passive, unproductive. It prolongs depression and impairs problem solving (Nolen-Hoeksema et al. 2008).

askFuture.label: Ask how he sees the next year or two

effects.log: You ask how he sees the future.

effects.finding: "What future? I'm 52. Who hires a 52-year-old printer? It's not going to get better."

effects.log: Hopelessness: one of the strongest markers of suicide risk (Beck et al. 1985). Ask about suicide directly.

screenPhq.label: With his agreement, give the PHQ-9 and go through it with him

effects.log: You give the PHQ-9 and go through his answers together.

effects.finding: He scores 17, moderately severe. On item 9, thoughts of being better off dead, he marked 'several days'.

askSuicide.label: Ask him directly whether he has had thoughts of suicide or of being better off dead
askSuicide.available: not talking and (not siKnown and not siDenied)

effects.log: You ask directly, calmly, about thoughts of suicide.

then.finding: A long pause. "Sometimes I think my wife would be better off without me. Then I think of the kids."

then.log: Passive thoughts of death; follow up now.

then.finding: "No. I'm not crazy." (He is not ready to say more.)

askIntent.label: Ask whether he has any intention of acting on those thoughts, or has thought about how, without asking for details
askIntent.available: not talking and (siKnown and not intentAsked)

effects.log: You ask about intent and planning, without asking for details.

effects.finding: "No. I'd never do that to them. I haven't thought about how. It's more like wishing I could disappear."

askPast.label: Ask whether he has ever tried to end his life, or come close
askPast.available: not talking and (siKnown and not pastAsked)

effects.log: You ask about past attempts.

askMeans.label: Ask whether there is anything at home he has thought of using to harm himself, without asking what
askMeans.available: not talking and (siKnown and not meansAsked)

effects.log: You ask, without asking for details, whether anything at home has been part of those thoughts.

effects.finding: "No. Nothing like that. It's just the thoughts."

askSupports.label: Ask who he talks to and what has kept him going

effects.log: You ask about the people in his life and his reasons for living.

effects.finding: "My kids. My brother Gary, I don't tell him much. My wife, Karen. She's the one who pushed me here."

safetyPlan.label: Write a short safety plan with him: his warning signs, what helps, people to call, and 988
safetyPlan.available: not talking and (siKnown and not safetyPlanned)

effects.log: You write a safety plan together in his words.

effects.finding: "Three a.m. replaying is the warning. Get up, walk the dog. Call Gary. 988 if it gets bad." He puts it in his phone.

effects.log: A collaborative safety plan, not a no-suicide contract (Stanley and Brown).

involveWife.label: Ask whether he will let you bring Karen in, briefly, to share the plan
involveWife.available: not talking and (safetyPlanned and not wifeInvolved)

effects.log: You ask his permission to involve his wife.

effects.finding: "Yeah. She's in the waiting room. She'll be relieved, honestly."

referMedical.label: Recommend a visit to his physician this week for his sleep, appetite and depression, including whether medication might help
referMedical.available: not talking and (symptomsHeard and not referMedical)

effects.log: You recommend a medical visit this week.

effects.finding: "I haven't seen a doctor in three years. Okay."

followUp.label: Schedule the next session in three days, not two weeks, and start activation: one small thing he used to enjoy

effects.log: You set a session in three days and one small step: an hour at the lake on Saturday.

effects.finding: "Friday. And the lake Saturday. With Gary, maybe."

reassure.label: Reassure him that things will turn around and he will find something soon

effects.log: You tell him things will get better soon.
Reassurance dismisses the hopelessness he just named, and hopelessness is what carries the risk.

debate.label: Argue with his hopelessness: list the reasons he should feel optimistic
debate.available: not talking and (hopeHeard and not debated)

effects.log: You argue that he has every reason to be optimistic.

sleepTips.label: Focus the session on sleep hygiene: no screens, a fixed wake time, no caffeine after noon

effects.log: You go through sleep hygiene tips.
You close the session.

Elevated, not imminent: passive thoughts, no intent, plan or past attempt, nothing at home; outpatient with a safety plan, his wife involved, a session in three days

risk.title: Predict (not scored)
risk.context: 'It's not going to get better.' He came in for stress and insomnia. What does this sentence change?

choices.label: Hopelessness carries real risk: ask about suicide directly, now

effects.log: Prediction: ask now.

choices.feedback: Right. Hopelessness predicted eventual suicide better than depression scores did in Beck's prospective study. Asking directly does not plant the idea; it opens the door.

choices.label: He needs encouragement: show him reasons for hope

effects.log: Prediction: encourage him.

choices.feedback: Encouragement before assessment dismisses what he said. Hear it, then ask about suicide directly.

choices.label: It is a first session; build rapport and ask in a few weeks

effects.log: Prediction: ask later.

choices.feedback: Risk is assessed at intake and throughout counseling. Hopelessness today is the reason to ask today.

formulation.question: Write your formulation: what you recognized behind 'stress and insomnia', the risk it carries, and your plan.

parts.label: Recognition
parts.criteria: Depressive symptoms (early waking, appetite, fatigue, anhedonia; PHQ-9 17) after a major loss; rumination (repetitive, unproductive replaying) that prolongs depression; hopelessness about the future, a strong risk marker.
parts.modelAnswer: Behind 'stress and insomnia' are depressive symptoms since his business closed: early waking, poor appetite, fatigue and loss of interest, with a PHQ-9 of 17. At night he ruminates, replaying decisions without solving anything, which keeps depression going. He is hopeless about the future, which is one of the strongest markers of suicide risk.

parts.label: Risk and plan
parts.criteria: Asked directly; passive thoughts of death, no intent or thoughts of how, no past attempt, nothing at home in the thoughts, protective ties; elevated not imminent; a safety plan, wife involved with consent, 988, physician this week, a session in three days, activation; no reassurance or debate.
parts.modelAnswer: I asked directly: he has passive thoughts that his wife would be better off without him, but no intent, no thoughts of how, no past attempt, and nothing at home has been part of the thoughts; his children are a strong reason to live. I judged his risk elevated but not imminent. We wrote a safety plan with 988, brought his wife in with his consent, and he will see his physician this week and me in three days, with one small activity on Saturday.

source.note: Rapport at the close of the session.
Asking about suicide within 20 minutes counts as timely: the intake form already names a major loss and he signals hopelessness early.

noProgress.rationale: Hopelessness after a major loss, and no direct question about suicide that he answered: his risk was never assessed.

expertPath.text: Check in and reflect; ask what else has changed and what goes through his mind at night.
Ask how he sees the future; hear the hopelessness; ask about suicide directly.
Follow up: intent, past attempts, anything at home, supports; give the PHQ-9.

heard.headline: Good: the depression behind the stress, and its risk
heard.body: You looked past 'stress and insomnia', heard rumination and hopelessness, asked about suicide directly while there was trust, and planned to the level of risk.

gaps.headline: Assessed, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria below show what was late or missing.

walkout.headline: He walked out
walkout.body: A man who came in only because his wife pushed him needs to feel heard. Arguing or brushing past him ends the session.

unassessed.headline: Risk never assessed
unassessed.body: Hopelessness after a major loss is the moment to ask about suicide, directly and once there is enough trust for an honest answer (Beck et al. 1985).

misread.headline: Depression read as stress
misread.body: Early waking, poor appetite, fatigue, lost interest, rumination and hopelessness are depression, and hopelessness carries risk. Two weeks and sleep tips do not fit.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Behind 'stress and insomnia' are depressive symptoms after a major loss (early waking, poor appetite, fatigue, anhedonia; PHQ-9 17), rumination that keeps depression going and impairs problem solving, and hopelessness, a strong marker of suicide risk. Ask about suicide directly once there is trust: he has passive thoughts of death, no intent or thoughts of how, no past attempt, nothing at home in the thoughts, and strong ties to his children. Elevated, not imminent: a collaborative safety plan with 988, his wife involved with consent, a physician visit this week, a session in three days, and behavioral activation. Do not reassure, debate, or treat only his sleep.
